title: April 2022 Class End of Block Exam

sets.title: Set 1: Original Exam Questions
sets.description: The original MCQs from the April 2022 class Block One Exam paper (PEN 101: Paediatrics Communicable Diseases, KRN September 2021 Class, Part A, Q1 to Q15).

questions.text: Normal milestones for a child aged 3 to 6 months include:

options.C: Can follow objects with their eyes
options.D: Can grasp small objects between thumb and fingers

questions.explanation: Can follow objects with their eyes (C) is correct because visual tracking develops in the first 3 months and is well established between 3 and 6 months. In this age range the baby also holds the head steady, turns towards sounds, laughs and squeals, reaches for and grasps a rattle with the whole hand, and begins to roll over. Standing with support (A) is a milestone of about 9 months. Sitting unsupported (B) is achieved at about 6 to 8 months, so it is not expected for the whole 3 to 6 month period (at 3 to 6 months the baby sits only with support). Grasping small objects between thumb and fingers, the pincer grasp (D), appears at about 9 to 12 months. Failure to follow objects with the eyes by 3 months is a reason to refer the child for developmental assessment.

questions.text: Baby N has a birth weight of 3.5kg. Her expected weight at 2 years would be:
questions.explanation: 14kg (D) is correct because a child's weight doubles by about 6 months and quadruples (4 times) by 2 years. Expected weight at 2 years = 3.5 kg x 4 = 14 kg. 4kg (A) is only a little above the birth weight and is far too low for a 2-year-old. 7kg (B) is the expected weight at about 6 months (3.5 x 2). 10.5kg (C) is three times the birth weight (3.5 x 3), expected at about 1 year. Weight is measured serially and charted on the child's health card, and is used to calculate Z-scores for nutritional status.

questions.text: Baby F presents with complaints of marked edema of the submandibular areas, dyspnea, barking cough and the mother reports to see a whitish, greyish matter at the back of the throat. The nurse suspects:
questions.explanation: Diphtheria (A) is correct because it is caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, whose exotoxin forms a greyish, adherent pseudo-membrane in the throat that bleeds when scraped. Marked swelling of the neck from lymphadenitis (bull's neck), difficulty breathing and a barking cough or stridor occur when the membrane and oedema narrow the airway; hoarseness, pain on swallowing and fever are also seen. Pertussis (B) causes paroxysmal coughing with a whoop and vomiting, with no throat membrane. Measles (C) causes fever, red watery eyes, runny nose, Koplik spots and a maculopapular rash, with a hacking cough but no throat membrane. Poliomyelitis (D) causes fever and flaccid paralysis, not a throat membrane. Nursing priorities are isolation (droplet precautions), humidified oxygen, readiness for an emergency tracheostomy, and giving diphtheria antitoxin and antibiotics (penicillin or erythromycin).

questions.text: Master S presents with a low grade fever, puffy cheeks and pain when they drink acidic juices. The likely diagnosis for Master S is:
questions.explanation: Mumps (B) is correct because it is a paramyxovirus infection whose hallmark is tender swelling of the parotid (salivary) glands, which gives the child puffy cheeks, with low-grade fever, headache, malaise and pain on chewing or swallowing. Acidic foods and drinks such as citrus juices stimulate saliva flow and make the swollen glands more painful, which is why they are avoided. Pertussis (A) presents with paroxysmal cough and a whoop. Poliomyelitis (C) presents with fever followed by flaccid paralysis. Diphtheria (D) presents with a grey throat membrane and bull's neck rather than swollen cheeks. Management is supportive: rest, fluids, soft non-acidic foods, paracetamol or ibuprofen, warm or cold compresses to the glands, and isolation for 5 days after the parotitis begins. Complications include orchitis, meningitis, pancreatitis and deafness; MMR vaccine prevents it.

questions.text: Management of a child who has latent TB infection involves:

options.B: Commencing first line Anti TB drugs
options.D: Withholding treatment until obvious TB symptoms present

questions.explanation: Administering prophylactic Isoniazid therapy (C) is correct because in latent TB infection the child carries the bacilli but has no symptoms and no active disease, so the aim is to prevent progression to TB disease. This is done with isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) at 10 mg/kg/day for 6 months, together with pyridoxine (vitamin B6) to prevent isoniazid peripheral neuropathy. Performing a Mantoux test (A) is a way of detecting infection (positive if induration is 10 mm or more, or 5 mm or more in a malnourished or HIV-infected child) and is not the management. Commencing first-line anti-TB drugs (B) (RHZE for 2 months then RH for 4 months) is the treatment of active TB disease. Withholding treatment until symptoms appear (D) is incorrect because children, especially those under 5 years and those with HIV, progress quickly to active disease. Children on IPT should not receive BCG until 2 weeks after completing the course.

questions.text: The mode of transmission for poliomyelitis is through:
questions.explanation: Oral – oral (A) is the best answer because poliovirus is an enteric virus spread from person to person by the faecal-oral route: the source is the faeces and oropharyngeal secretions of infected people (especially young children), and the virus is taken in by mouth, so the oral route is the entry point. The virus persists about 1 week in the throat and 4 to 6 weeks in the faeces, and it is spread where sanitation and hygiene are poor. Cough droplets (B) and suspended particles in the air (C) describe respiratory (droplet and airborne) transmission as in pertussis, diphtheria, measles and chickenpox. Fomites (D) are contaminated articles and are only a minor, indirect route. Note: the examiner's phrase 'oral - oral' is best read as the faecal-oral/oral route, which is why it is the closest option to the lecture content. Prevention is by IPV and OPV, good hygiene, safe disposal of stool, and surveillance for acute flaccid paralysis (AFP).

questions.text: Using ETAT triage the following children first to last. Baby W 1.5 months old who has come for vaccination, Baby K epistaxis, Baby R edema of lower limbs
questions.explanation: K, R, W (B) is correct. In ETAT (Emergency Triage, Assessment and Treatment) children are sorted into emergency signs, priority signs and non-urgent. Baby K has active bleeding (epistaxis), which needs immediate attention to stop the bleeding and to check for shock, so K is seen first. Baby R has oedema of the feet, which is a priority sign (the 'O' in the mnemonic 3 TPR - MOB, oedema of both feet, suggesting severe malnutrition), so R goes to the front of the queue after any emergency case. Baby W is 1.5 months old, and 'tiny baby' is a priority sign only when the baby is sick; W has come for vaccination, is not sick and has no emergency or priority signs, so W is non-urgent and waits his turn last. A, C and D are wrong because they place the well baby W before a child who is bleeding or has a priority sign, and triage must never delay a sick child. Triage is done as soon as the child arrives, before registration.

questions.text: A true statement regarding polio virus is:

options.A: About 24% of the infected cases progress to flaccid paralysis
options.B: Abortive polio leads to paralysis of the limbs
options.C: A common complication of polio is severe melena
options.D: All children who contract polio recover fully

questions.explanation: About 24% of the infected cases progress to flaccid paralysis (A) is the option the examiner intends as the true statement, and it is chosen here by elimination because the other three are clearly false. Poliovirus infection mainly affects the anterior-horn motor neurons and causes flaccid, asymmetrical paralysis in the paralytic form. Caution: the lecture notes state that only about 1 in 200 infections (0.5%) leads to irreversible paralysis, and that 90 to 95% of infections are inapparent, so the figure of 24% in this option is not accurate and the item is poorly worded; check it against the marking scheme. Abortive polio (B) is the minor, flu-like illness with no CNS involvement, which resolves in 24 to 72 hours and does not cause paralysis. Severe melena (C) is not a complication of polio; the complications are paralysis, respiratory arrest and kidney stones from bone demineralisation during prolonged immobility. All children recover fully (D) is false because the paralytic type leaves permanent disability of varying degree, and mortality is 1 to 4%, higher in bulbar polio.

questions.text: A common complication of chicken pox is:
questions.explanation: Secondary bacterial infection (D) is correct because the itchy vesicles are scratched, which breaks the skin and lets skin bacteria (Staphylococcus and Streptococcus) enter, causing impetigo, cellulitis and abscesses. It is the most common complication of chickenpox and is prevented by keeping the nails short, using mittens, calamine lotion and antihistamines, and keeping the skin clean. Encephalitis (A) is a recognised complication of chickenpox but it is uncommon. Reye syndrome (B) is rare and is linked to giving aspirin during a viral illness, so aspirin must be avoided. Orchitis (C) is a complication of mumps and not of chickenpox. Other chickenpox complications are pneumonia, dehydration and bleeding problems.

questions.text: The pathognomic characteristics of measles infection is:
questions.explanation: Koplik spot (C) is correct because Koplik spots, tiny white spots (like grains of salt) on a red base inside the mouth opposite the molars, are pathognomonic for measles, meaning they occur in no other disease and confirm the diagnosis. They appear 2 to 3 days after the symptoms begin and 1 to 2 days before the rash. High fever (A) occurs in many infections and is not specific. Coryza, a runny nose (B), with red watery eyes and cough, is part of the prodromal stage but is also found in common colds and other illnesses. The macular papular rash (D) is typical of measles (starting behind the ears and forehead and spreading downwards, sparing the palms and soles), but similar rashes occur in rubella, drug reactions and other viral infections. Management is supportive, with vitamin A supplementation, isolation under airborne precautions, and treatment of complications.

questions.text: Baby V present with hypothermia, constipation, old man face, hanging skin but has a voracious appetite when offered food to eat. Baby V's diagnosis is likely to be:
questions.explanation: Marasmus (B) is correct because it is a severe form of protein-energy malnutrition caused mainly by a prolonged lack of energy (calories). The body uses up its fat and muscle, so the child has severe wasting with an 'old man' (wizened) face, loose skin hanging in folds (the 'baggy pants' appearance), prominent ribs, and no oedema. Hypothermia occurs because there is no body fat for insulation, and the child is typically alert and irritable with a good, even voracious, appetite. Underweight baby (A) means low weight for age without the features of severe wasting. Marasmic kwashiorkor (C) combines severe wasting with bilateral pitting oedema, which Baby V does not have. Kwashiorkor (D) is dominated by bilateral pitting oedema, flaky-paint skin changes, sparse reddish hair, a moon face, an enlarged fatty liver, apathy and poor appetite, and the child may look well fed because the oedema hides the wasting.

questions.text: Indication for admission for a child with a diagnosis of Protein Energy Malnutrition (PEM) is:
questions.explanation: Failing the appetite test (B) is correct because a child with severe acute malnutrition who fails the appetite test (cannot or will not take the ready-to-use therapeutic food) has complicated malnutrition and must be admitted for inpatient stabilisation. Children who pass the appetite test, are alert and clinically well can be treated as outpatients. Other indications for admission are bilateral pitting oedema of severe degree (+++), any general danger sign or medical complication (for example pneumonia, severe dehydration, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, high fever, severe anaemia), and age under 6 months. Availability of a caregiver (A) is not a medical indication for admission. Absence of lesions (C) is not an indication, since the child is only admitted when there are complications. Pitting oedema grade one (D) is mild (+) and a child with mild oedema who has a good appetite and no complications can be managed as an outpatient; it is the severe oedema (+++) that requires admission.

questions.text: The specific nursing management in first 2 days of admission for a child diagnosed with PEM is:

options.A: Preparing for follow up, initiating sensory stimulation
options.B: Monitoring catch up growth, assuring of cautious feeding

questions.explanation: Preventing dehydration, preventing hypoglycemia (D) is correct because the first 2 days of the stabilisation phase of the WHO 10-step management of severe malnutrition target the immediate life-threatening problems: (1) hypoglycaemia, (2) hypothermia and (3) dehydration. Hypoglycaemia is prevented by feeding or giving 10% glucose or sucrose immediately on admission and then feeding every 2 hours day and night. Dehydration is treated cautiously with ReSoMal (oral or by NG tube) and not with aggressive IV fluids, which can cause heart failure, except in shock. Preparing for follow up and initiating sensory stimulation (A) belong to the rehabilitation phase (weeks 2 to 6) and discharge. Monitoring catch-up growth (B) is a rehabilitation step, while cautious feeding with F-75 starts in the stabilisation phase but catch-up growth does not. Checking for infection and preventing hypothermia (C) are also part of stabilisation, but infection is treated from day 1 and continues to about day 7, so D is the combination that is specific to the first 2 days. Note: C and D both contain stabilisation steps, so check this item against the marking scheme.

questions.text: A risk factor for infection with Clostridium tetani is:

options.A: Home delivery by Traditional Birth Attendant
options.B: Lack of immunization of the mother with tetanus toxoid in third trimester
options.C: Application of chlorohexidine gel on the cord stump during cord care
options.D: Use of sterile scissors to cut the cord on delivery

questions.explanation: Home delivery by Traditional Birth Attendant (A) is correct because home deliveries are more likely to involve cutting the cord with dirty, unsterilised instruments, tying it with unsterile materials, no hand-washing by the provider, and dressing the stump with harmful substances such as herbs and dung, all of which let Clostridium tetani spores enter the umbilical cord and cause neonatal tetanus. Lack of tetanus toxoid immunisation of the mother (B) is a real risk factor, but the option specifies the third trimester only; according to the TT schedule, the doses are given from the 4th to the 8th month (second and third trimesters), so the lack of immunisation is the risk and not the timing in the third trimester alone, which makes A the more direct answer. Chlorhexidine gel on the stump (C) is a protective antiseptic cord-care practice. Use of sterile scissors (D) is a preventive measure (clean blade). Remember the three cleans: clean hands, clean blade and clean dressing of the cord.

questions.text: An isolation precaution for a child admitted with a diagnosis of Pertussis is:
questions.explanation: Droplet (C) is correct because Bordetella pertussis spreads through large droplets from the nasopharyngeal and bronchial secretions of an infected person during coughing, and freshly contaminated objects are also infective. Droplet precautions mean a single room or cohorting of cases, a surgical mask for anyone within about 1 metre, hand hygiene, and the patient wearing a mask when moved. The patient is infectious from 2 days before the cough starts for at least 3 weeks, and is most infectious in the catarrhal stage. Protective isolation (A) is used for patients who are immunosuppressed and need protection from infection. Airborne precautions (B) are used for diseases that spread through small particles that remain suspended in the air, such as measles, chickenpox and pulmonary TB. Contact precautions (D) are for infections spread by touching, such as cutaneous diphtheria and wound infections. Other care includes oxygen, gentle suction, a calm quiet environment, erythromycin (30 to 50 mg/kg QID for 10 days), and admission for severe illness or a child under 3 months.
